newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian euthanasia advocate designs "coma machine".
newsitem.headline: Australian euthanasia advocate designs "coma machine".

text.p: Leading Australian euthanasia campaigner Dr Philip Nitschke said on Wednesday he had designed a "coma machine" to give terminally ill patients a guarantee that they would never regain consciousness after an infusion of pain-killing drugs.

Nitschke, who helped four people die through computer-delivered injections under Australia's short-lived voluntary euthanasia laws, said his new device would expose the hypocrisy of laws which allowed doctors to induce death through drug infusions under the guise of treating pain.
"The analogy really here is the terminally ill are swimming and we are adding lead to them," Nitschke told the South Australia state Press Club.
"We keep on adding the lead and then they sink and we say they died of a disease...this is hypocritical and it needs to be shown for what it is," he said.
The Australian national parliament quashed the Northern Territory's world-first euthanasia law in March, nine months after it came into operation.
But Nitschke said there was a "grey area" between euthanasia and accepted medical practice that could be used to help the terminally ill die.
He said his coma machine, currently at prototype stage, would employ a computer-programmed sensor for consciousness and a control rate for an intravenous drip.

"It is a slightly macabre device...to provide the patient with the guarantee that they will not wake up, that if they ever look like waking up, it will be sensed, and more drugs at a faster rate will flow into that person," he said.

Nitschke faces police questioning over the death of a 56-year-old nurse, Esther Wild, who had met the requirements for voluntary euthanasia under the Northern Territory law only to see it quashed by parliament. Police in the outback Territory are preparing a report on Wild's death.

Nitschke said Wild, who died on April 17 after four days in a coma brought on by pain-relieving drugs, had been distressed to regain consciousness on the third day, calling out to a friend and asking: "Am I dead? Is this death?"
"It seemed like we were suspending her like a fine thread, hanging her between life and death, loading her up until the thread broke," he said.

"If it is considered to be good medical practice to allow a person to die over two days and yet if you increase the infusion rate and they die over two hours it is considered to be murder," he said. "Clearly there is a grey area somewhere between those two extremes. The need now is to move into that grey area."

The legal cloud surrounding the issue was immediately apparent when South Australia's senior legal official, Paul Rofe, attended Nitschke's appearance in Adelaide and said his description of Wild's death amounted to a murder confession.
"I did not expect to come along here today and hear what I believe to be technically a confession to the murder of Esther Wild," Rofe, the state's Director of Public Prosecutions, told reporters.
"I believe I did, in strict legal terms," he said. But he said he did not believe any jury in Australia would convict Nitschke.
